blocks.text: 1. Naive Bayes

blocks.alt: Features feed Bayes theorem to produce a class probability

blocks.text: Logistic Regression fits a linear boundary and KNN votes among nearby stored points, but Naive Bayes takes a genuinely different, fully probabilistic route to classification. It is built directly on Bayes theorem, a foundational rule from probability theory for updating a belief once new evidence arrives, combined with one deliberately simplifying assumption that gives the algorithm its name. The result is a classifier that trains in a single fast pass over the data, needs comparatively little training data to work well, and remains, despite its simplicity, a genuinely strong baseline for text classification tasks like spam filtering.

Where Logistic Regression is a discriminative model, meaning it learns the boundary between classes directly without ever modeling how the data itself was generated, Naive Bayes is a generative model. It explicitly models how each class tends to produce its features, then uses that model to work backward and figure out which class most plausibly generated the observed features of a new example. This generative framing is what makes it fast to train, since fitting the model is mostly a matter of counting frequencies rather than running an iterative optimizer.
2. Bayes Theorem

blocks.alt: A prior times a likelihood produces a posterior

blocks.text: Bayes theorem describes exactly how to update a belief given new evidence. In classification terms, it starts with a prior, the probability of a class before looking at any features at all, simply how common that class is in the overall population. It also uses a likelihood, the probability of observing the given features assuming the example truly belongs to that class. Bayes theorem combines these into a posterior, the probability of the class given the observed features, which is precisely the quantity a classifier needs to predict.

Formally, the posterior is proportional to the prior multiplied by the likelihood, divided by a normalizing constant that ensures probabilities across all classes sum to one. For the purpose of picking the single most likely class, that normalizing constant can actually be ignored entirely, since it is identical across every candidate class and does not change which one scores highest. This is a crucial simplification that Naive Bayes relies on in practice.

blocks.text: 3. The Naive Independence Assumption

blocks.alt: Feature A and feature B are assumed independent

blocks.text: Computing the true likelihood of an entire set of features given a class, accounting for every possible interaction and correlation between features, is generally intractable, requiring an amount of data that grows exponentially with the number of features. Naive Bayes sidesteps this entirely with one bold, deliberately simplifying assumption: every feature is treated as conditionally independent of every other feature, given the class label.

This assumption is almost never exactly true of real data. In a spam filter, the words free and winner are far more likely to appear together in the same spam email than independence would predict, since spam emails often use several suspicious words at once rather than just one. Naive Bayes ignores this correlation entirely and treats each word as if it contributed independent evidence. This is precisely the naive in the algorithm name. Remarkably, despite this assumption frequently being false, Naive Bayes classifiers remain competitive in practice on many real tasks, because what matters for classification is getting the relative ranking between classes right, not the exact probability values.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: The independence assumption being technically false does not always hurt accuracy much, since Naive Bayes only needs to rank the correct class highest, not compute perfectly calibrated probabilities. It does mean the raw predicted probabilities themselves are often overconfident and should not be trusted at face value.

blocks.text: 4. Making a Prediction

With the independence assumption in place, predicting the class of a new example becomes a simple product. For each candidate class, multiply that class’s prior probability by the likelihood of every individual observed feature given that class. Because the features are assumed independent given the class, the joint likelihood of all of them together collapses into a plain product of each feature’s individual likelihood, something that can be estimated directly from counts in the training data.

This calculation is repeated once per candidate class, producing one score per class. The predicted class is simply whichever one produced the highest score. Note that these scores are not full probabilities, since the normalizing constant from Bayes theorem was dropped, but that omission does not matter because only the relative ranking across classes is needed to make a prediction.
5. Three Common Variants

blocks.alt: Naive Bayes comes in Gaussian, Multinomial, and Bernoulli variants

blocks.text: Naive Bayes is not one single algorithm but a family, distinguished by what assumption each variant makes about how features are distributed within each class. Gaussian Naive Bayes assumes each continuous feature follows a normal, bell-shaped distribution within each class, estimating just a mean and variance per feature per class from the training data, well suited to measurements like sensor readings or physical dimensions.

Multinomial Naive Bayes instead models feature values as counts, making it the classic choice for text classification where features are word frequencies within a document. Bernoulli Naive Bayes is similar but tracks only whether a feature occurred at all, a binary presence or absence, rather than how many times, which suits short texts or features that are naturally binary. Choosing the right variant for the shape of the actual feature data matters a great deal for how well the independence assumption and the distributional assumption together hold up.

blocks.text: 6. Naive Bayes for Text Classification

Text classification is where Naive Bayes has earned its long-standing reputation, and it connects directly back to the Text Features topic in the Feature Engineering module. A document is represented as a bag of words, essentially a count of how many times each vocabulary term appears, discarding word order. Multinomial Naive Bayes treats each word count as a small piece of independent evidence for or against each candidate class.

In a spam filter, words like free, winner, and click tend to appear far more frequently in spam emails than in legitimate ones, so their presence pushes the posterior probability of the spam class up relative to the ham, or legitimate, class. Multiplying together the evidence from every word in the email, even under the admittedly false independence assumption, produces a surprisingly reliable spam score. Because training amounts to little more than counting word frequencies per class, Naive Bayes can be trained on very large text corpora extremely quickly, something that matters when a spam filter needs to be retrained frequently to keep up with new spam tactics.
7. The Zero Probability Problem

blocks.alt: An unseen word in training gives a zero probability, fixed by Laplace smoothing

blocks.text: A subtle but serious problem arises whenever a feature value never appeared alongside a particular class during training. If the word cryptocurrency was never seen in any spam email in the training set, the raw estimated likelihood of that word given spam is exactly zero. Because Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods together, a single zero in that product wipes out the entire class score to zero, no matter how strong the evidence from every other word in the email happens to be.

The standard fix is Laplace smoothing, also called additive smoothing, which adds a small constant, typically 1, to every observed count before computing probabilities. This guarantees every feature-class combination gets a small nonzero probability, even ones never observed during training, without meaningfully distorting the probabilities for combinations that were observed frequently. Nearly every practical Naive Bayes implementation, including scikit-learn’s, applies Laplace smoothing by default.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: The smoothing constant is often called alpha in library implementations. The default of 1 works well in most cases, but it is a tunable hyperparameter, and a smaller alpha can help when the training data is large enough that zero counts are rare and genuinely meaningful.

blocks.text: 8. Working in Log Space

blocks.alt: Tiny probabilities multiplied together move into log space for stable addition instead

blocks.text: Multiplying together many probabilities, each already a fraction less than one, one per feature in the dataset, produces a result that shrinks toward zero extremely fast as the number of features grows. With enough features, this product can underflow the numeric precision of standard floating point arithmetic, effectively becoming zero for every class and making it impossible to tell which class actually scored highest.

The practical fix is to work in log space instead of raw probability space. Since the logarithm of a product equals the sum of the logarithms of its factors, the entire prior-times-likelihood-product calculation can be replaced with a sum of log prior plus the sum of log likelihoods. Sums of moderately sized negative numbers are numerically stable in a way that products of many small fractions are not, and because the logarithm function is monotonically increasing, the class with the highest log score is still exactly the class with the highest raw score. Every serious Naive Bayes implementation performs this calculation in log space internally.
9. Naive Bayes versus Logistic Regression

blocks.alt: Naive Bayes is generative while logistic regression is discriminative

blocks.text: Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression are often compared directly because they can both be applied to the same binary or multiclass classification problems, yet they represent two philosophically distinct approaches. Naive Bayes is generative, modeling how each class produces its features and working backward via Bayes theorem, while Logistic Regression is discriminative, modeling the boundary between classes directly without ever describing how the features themselves arose.

In practice, Naive Bayes trains dramatically faster, since fitting it requires only counting frequencies in a single pass, whereas Logistic Regression needs an iterative optimization process to converge via maximum likelihood estimation. Naive Bayes also tends to need less training data to reach a reasonable performance level, because its strong independence assumption effectively reduces the number of parameters that need to be estimated. Logistic Regression, by making fewer structural assumptions about how features relate to one another, often edges out Naive Bayes in raw accuracy once enough training data is available, particularly when features are strongly correlated, exactly the situation where the naive independence assumption is most clearly violated.
10. Worked Example
The example below builds a small Multinomial Naive Bayes spam classifier from raw text, using the same bag-of-words vectorization approach covered in the Text Features topic.

code.content:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report

emails = [
    "win free money now click here", "you have won a free prize claim now",
    "cheap loans no credit check needed", "free entry win big cash prize",
    "meeting scheduled for tomorrow morning", "please review the attached report",
    "lunch with the team at noon today", "project deadline moved to next friday",
]
labels = [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]  # 1 = spam, 0 = not spam

vectorizer = CountVectorizer()
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(emails)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, labels, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

model = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)  # alpha=1.0 applies Laplace smoothing
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

predictions = model.predict(X_test)
probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_test)

print("Predictions:", predictions)
print("Spam probabilities:", probabilities[:, 1])
print("Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_test, predictions))
print(classification_report(y_test, predictions, target_names=["not spam", "spam"]))

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: CountVectorizer builds the bag-of-words matrix automatically, one column per vocabulary term. MultinomialNB then treats each column count as independent evidence, exactly the process described conceptually throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Naive Bayes is a generative, probabilistic classifier built directly on Bayes theorem: posterior proportional to prior times likelihood.
The naive independence assumption treats every feature as conditionally independent given the class, rarely true but computationally powerful.
Prediction scores each candidate class by prior times the product of per-feature likelihoods, then picks the highest score.
Gaussian, Multinomial, and Bernoulli variants fit continuous, count-based, and binary feature data respectively.
Multinomial Naive Bayes on bag-of-words features is a classic, fast, competitive baseline for text and spam classification.
Laplace smoothing prevents a single unseen feature value from zeroing out an entire class prediction.
Real implementations sum log probabilities rather than multiplying raw probabilities, to avoid numeric underflow.
Compared to Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes trains faster and needs less data, but Logistic Regression often wins with more data and correlated features.
